title: How AI learned to love the Chinese Communist Party
gist: Zuckerman argues the bigger AI risk than extinction is erosion of informed democracy: a study finds LLMs (including US models Claude and ChatGPT) echo Chinese state propaganda because state media dominates Chinese-language training corpora, with spillover into Japanese, Korean and English. Meanwhile AI undercuts the economics of reporting while making propaganda cheap, and publishers are walling off content from scrapers.

insights.claim: A study titled 'State media control influences large language models' found that LLMs of all kinds, closed and open, routinely return Chinese government-sponsored propaganda, especially when prompted in Chinese.
insights.speaker: Ethan Zuckerman
insights.so_what: Model outputs on sensitive geopolitical topics are shaped by corpus composition, a reputational and regulatory risk for AI vendors.
insights.quote: they found that large language models of all kinds routinely returned government-sponsored propaganda, especially when prompted in Chinese

insights.claim: Pro-Beijing responses appear not only in Chinese-built models like DeepSeek but also in US-based models including Claude and ChatGPT, via training data rather than direct censorship.
insights.speaker: Ethan Zuckerman
insights.so_what: US labs cannot claim neutrality on China topics; exposes them to political scrutiny in Washington.
insights.quote: But these responses were also found in US-based models including Claude and ChatGPT.

insights.claim: Chinese state media documents are more than ten times as prevalent in training corpora as Chinese Wikipedia or Baidu's encyclopedia.
insights.speaker: Ethan Zuckerman
insights.so_what: Quantifies how state-funded content volume translates into model influence.
insights.quote: more than ten times more prevalent than those from Chinese Wikipedia or the commercial encyclopedia from Chinese company Baidu

insights.claim: A 'spillover' effect means languages sharing tokens with Chinese, notably Japanese and Korean, also show significant pro-government bias, and it appears in English too.
insights.speaker: Ethan Zuckerman
insights.so_what: Information-influence operations can propagate across languages through shared model internals, widening geopolitical exposure.

insights.claim: When asked questions in languages of less-than-open societies such as Vietnamese or Turkmen, AIs are more likely to give pro-government than critical answers because state media is abundant and independent voices are scarce.
insights.speaker: Ethan Zuckerman
insights.so_what: Authoritarian states can effectively 'own' the model view of themselves in their own language.

insights.claim: For common questions, human feedback steers models to verified answers, but niche questions are answered by inference from training documents, where biased source mix dominates.
insights.speaker: Ethan Zuckerman
insights.so_what: Long-tail queries are where model reliability and bias risk concentrate.

insights.claim: Repression that removes critical content offline and online (e.g. forcing YouTube takedowns, jailing activists) effectively rigs the information environment that AI learns from.
insights.speaker: Ethan Zuckerman
insights.so_what: Censorship upstream now has a multiplier effect via AI.

themes.theme: Economics of truth vs cheap propaganda

insights.claim: AI answers are undercutting the advertising revenue that funds expensive fact-establishing journalism, since users no longer click through search links.
insights.speaker: Ethan Zuckerman
insights.so_what: Structural headwind for ad-funded publishers; pressure for licensing deals with AI labs.
insights.quote: Why follow a search engine link to a report, and view some ads in the process, when an AI will give a plausible answer on the spot?

insights.claim: The cost asymmetry between producing AI-generated narrative content and doing actual reporting is widening, favouring propagandists.
insights.speaker: Ethan Zuckerman
insights.so_what: Information quality in model inputs will likely degrade, raising value of verified, licensed data.
insights.quote: It costs very little to publish waves of AI-generated content promoting a particular narrative, and vastly more to carry out the reporting necessary

insights.claim: In 2024 French researchers uncovered the 'Pravda network', a large set of AI-powered pro-Kremlin news sites designed to inject narratives into LLMs and Wikipedia (LLM grooming).
insights.speaker: Ethan Zuckerman
insights.so_what: State actors are already deliberately poisoning training data.

insights.claim: Credible outlets are blocking AI training bots, and Global Voices had to bar traffic from whole nations after aggressive scraping knocked its site offline; this makes quality content less accessible while propaganda floods in.
insights.speaker: Ethan Zuckerman
insights.so_what: Bot-blocking and paywalls shift the training-data mix further toward low-quality and propaganda sources.
